description: Why technologies get adopted or rejected, how to weigh evidence and causal claims, and the ethics and governance ideas behind rules, platforms and automated decisions, for an architect making adoption and policy calls.

notes.front: Name Rogers' five perceived attributes that predict an innovation's adoption rate, and say which direction of each helps adoption.
notes.back: Relative advantage (higher), compatibility with existing values and workflows (higher), complexity (lower), trialability (higher), observability of results (higher).
notes.extra: In practice: Score your platform on each. Low trialability (two-week onboarding) and low observability (nobody sees other teams' wins) are common, cheap-to-fix adoption killers.

notes.front: Name Rogers' five adopter categories in order of adoption, and what separates the earliest from the latest.
notes.back: Innovators → early adopters → early majority → late majority → laggards. Earlier groups tolerate risk and incompleteness; later groups need proof, peer examples and low risk.
notes.extra: Roughly 2.5 / 13.5 / 34 / 34 / 16% (a normal-curve modelling choice, not a law). In practice: Your first platform teams are innovators; don't extrapolate their enthusiasm to the whole company.

notes.front: Moore's chasm: where does it sit, and why does adoption stall there?
notes.back: Between early adopters (visionaries who tolerate incompleteness) and the early majority (pragmatists who want a proven whole product and references from peers like them). Visionaries aren't references for pragmatists.
notes.extra: In practice: Platform adoption stalls around 15%: the next teams want case studies, migration support and guarantees. Cross by nailing one narrow niche completely.

notes.front: A product delights early adopters but sales stall. What must change to cross the chasm?
notes.back: Stop selling to enthusiasts and target one niche of pragmatists with a whole product (complete, supported, integrated) and references from peers in that niche.

notes.front: Diffusion research: what actually drives the decision to adopt: information availability or peers' visible results?
notes.back: Peers' visible results. People hear about an innovation from promoters but decide by watching neighbours like themselves succeed with it; interpersonal networks govern the pace.
notes.extra: Example: Iowa farmers took years to adopt clearly superior hybrid corn, switching once neighbours' yields were visible.

notes.front: What best explains how fast a group adopts a clearly useful innovation?
notes.back: Expected profitability for the adopter. Adoption follows an S-curve whose timing and slope track the economic gain, more than education or access to information.
notes.extra: Example: Hybrid corn spread fastest in the states where the gain per acre was highest. In practice: Make the payoff per team concrete.

notes.front: Why do some innovations spread within a year while equally valid ones take decades?
notes.back: Fast: the benefit is immediate, visible, and accrues to the adopter. Slow: the mechanism is invisible, the benefit is delayed or goes to someone else, and the adopter bears tedious effort.
notes.extra: Example: Anaesthesia (surgeon sees the effect at once) spread in a year; antisepsis (infection appears days later) took ~20.

notes.front: Beyond specs and price, what can block adoption of a working technology?
notes.back: Social acceptability: if use is visible and breaks norms (privacy, status, etiquette), people and venues reject it regardless of capability.
notes.extra: Example: Google Glass: face-mounted cameras violated privacy norms; retreated to enterprise use.

notes.front: What is 'worse is better', and what does it say about adoption?
notes.back: Systems that are simple to implement, even if incomplete or inconsistent, spread faster than 'the right thing', because they are easy to port, understand and improve incrementally.
notes.extra: Example: Unix and C beat more principled designs. In practice: Implementation simplicity is an adoption feature of a platform API.

notes.front: What do standards do for diffusion?
notes.back: They reduce buyer risk (no orphaned investment), create markets for complements (parts, training, tooling), and add network effects across suppliers. Standards wars are usually won by installed base and openness, not technical merit.
notes.extra: Example: ISO containers, GSM, TCP/IP over OSI.

notes.front: VHS beat technically better Betamax. What general lesson does that teach?
notes.back: Openness plus the use case the buyer cares about wins: liberal licensing brought more makers and lower prices, longer recording fit the key use (a full film), and content network effects tipped the market.

notes.front: State Amara's law.
notes.back: We overestimate a technology's effect in the short run and underestimate it in the long run.
notes.extra: In practice: Expect a disappointment phase after the launch hype; don't cancel a platform that is still in its J-curve dip.

notes.front: The Gartner hype cycle: what are its stages, and what is its epistemic status?
notes.back: Trigger → peak of inflated expectations → trough of disillusionment → slope of enlightenment → plateau. It is a heuristic, not a validated regularity: many technologies die in the trough or never peak.

notes.front: Why do general-purpose technologies take decades to show productivity gains?
notes.back: The gains need complementary reorganisation (layouts, workflows, skills, management), not just the core technology. Redesigning around it is the bottleneck.
notes.extra: Example: Electric motors paid off only when factories dropped steam-era line shafts for a motor per machine, ~40 years after power stations. In practice: Lift-and-shift to cloud without changing ops and org captures little.
notes.source: Paul David, 'The Dynamo and the Computer'

notes.front: What is the productivity J-curve?
notes.back: A general-purpose technology needs large intangible investments (process redesign, skills, data) that aren't counted as output while being made, so measured productivity first dips, then rises above trend.
notes.extra: The Solow paradox ('computers everywhere but in the productivity statistics') is this dip at national scale. In practice: Expect a 'nothing is working' phase in any platform or AI rollout.

notes.front: What does AC's victory over DC teach about technology contests?
notes.back: Cost structure beats narrative. Transformers let AC travel long distances cheaply; DC served ~1–2 km. Safety propaganda against AC didn't change the outcome.
notes.extra: In practice: In a platform debate, model the unit economics; marketing claims rarely decide the outcome.

notes.front: What is the sailing ship effect?
notes.back: Incumbent technologies often improve fastest after a challenger appears. The incumbent's response can delay the transition for decades without preventing it.
notes.extra: Example: Sail improved most under pressure from steam. In practice: Expect the legacy vendor's best offer right after you announce the migration.

notes.front: Christensen's disruptive innovation: what is the mechanism, and the main caveat?
notes.back:
Entrants start worse on mainstream metrics but cheaper or simpler, serving overlooked customers; incumbents rationally ignore them, then the entrant improves into the mainstream.
Caveat: weak predictive record; many incumbents adapt.

notes.front: Teece: when an innovation is easy to copy, who captures the profit?
notes.back: Whoever controls the complementary assets: manufacturing, distribution, service, brand.
notes.extra: Example: EMI invented the CT scanner but lacked US sales and service; GE took the market. In practice: Your internal platform's moat is support and integration, not the code.

notes.front: What does Xerox PARC teach about adoption inside a firm?
notes.back: Firms commercialise what fits their existing business model and sales channel, not what is technically best. Xerox sold the laser printer (fit the copier business) and left the GUI to others.
notes.extra: In practice: An internal innovation needs an owner whose incentives and channels it fits.

notes.front: What is the main risk of a very long build cycle for a new technology?
notes.back: Frozen market assumptions: the world changes while you build, and the addressable market can vanish before launch.
notes.extra: Example: Iridium's satellite phone launched after cellular coverage had already eaten its market. In practice: Ship thin slices and re-validate demand.

notes.front: How can an early success become a later trap (the Minitel lesson)?
notes.back: A successful installed base and business model create lock-in that delays adoption of the next, better technology.
notes.extra: Example: France's Minitel videotex network slowed French internet adoption for years. In practice: Today's successful internal platform can become tomorrow's legacy.

notes.front: Why did shipping containers take ~15 years to take off, though the box itself was trivial?
notes.back: Adoption needed standards (ISO sizes), complementary infrastructure (cranes, ships, rail) and labour settlements. Then freight costs collapsed.
notes.extra: In practice: Container platforms likewise need standards, tooling and an operating-model deal with ops teams, not just the runtime.

notes.front: Once a technology is proven to work, what is usually the remaining adoption bottleneck?
notes.back: Unit cost and manufacturability. A proof of concept that can't be produced cheaply loses to a cruder, cheaper alternative.
notes.extra: Example: Marine chronometers solved longitude, but became standard only after simplified designs made them affordable.

notes.front: What is the Jevons paradox (rebound effect)?
notes.back: Making a resource more efficient lowers its effective price and can increase total consumption. Efficiency alone is not a conservation strategy.
notes.extra: In practice: Cheaper compute per request (or cheaper LLM tokens) often raises the total bill. Pair efficiency with budgets or quotas.

notes.front: What is Wright's law, and what decides the learning rate?
notes.back: Unit cost falls by a fixed percentage for each doubling of cumulative production. The rate is a property of the production system: standardised, repeated builds learn (solar ~20%/doubling); bespoke builds may not (nuclear got costlier).
notes.extra: In practice: Standardise platform components so each new cluster or tenant gets cheaper.

notes.front: In what sense was Moore's law self-fulfilling?
notes.back: It worked as a coordination device: a shared roadmap told suppliers, fabs and customers what to target and when, aligning investment. An expectation that coordinates investment can create the regularity it predicts.

notes.front: Perez: what are the two phases of a technological revolution, and what separates them?
notes.back: Installation (financial-capital frenzy, bubble) → turning point (crash, institutional reset) → deployment (production capital, broad diffusion).

notes.front: How can a single vivid failure shape a whole technology's future?
notes.back: One legible catastrophe can end a technology or trigger a regulatory ratchet that governs all later adoption in the sector, regardless of the actuarial safety record.
notes.extra: Example: The Hindenburg ended passenger airships; thalidomide made proof of efficacy mandatory for all drugs. In practice: One bad platform outage can set adoption back years.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: What is the Semmelweis reflex?
notes.back: Reflexive rejection of evidence that contradicts established norms, especially when it comes without a mechanism, from an outsider, or implies the experts were at fault.
notes.extra: Example: Hand-washing cut maternal deaths ~9× but was rejected until germ theory supplied a mechanism.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: Why can strong correlational evidence still fail to convince a field?
notes.back: Without a plausible mechanism it is easy to dismiss. Acceptance typically follows a mechanism plus a decisive new dataset.
notes.extra: Example: Continental drift was rejected for 50 years until seafloor spreading supplied the mechanism. In practice: Pair your metrics with the 'why'.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: How can a working practice silently drift into a non-working one?
notes.back: If nobody knows why it works, a 'harmless' substitution can remove the active ingredient unnoticed.
notes.extra: Example: The Navy cured scurvy with lemons, then switched to limes (much less vitamin C) and scurvy returned. In practice: Runbook steps copied without understanding rot the same way.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: What is Planck's principle, and is there evidence for it?
notes.back: 'Science advances one funeral at a time.' Yes: after a star scientist dies, outsiders enter and cite more in the subfield. Incumbency effects on ideas are real.
notes.extra: In practice: Sometimes a new architecture direction needs new owners, not better arguments.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: What is the Collingridge dilemma?
notes.back: Early on, a technology's impacts are unpredictable but it's easy to change; once impacts are clear it is entrenched and hard to change. Governance must act under uncertainty or not at all.
notes.extra: In practice: Set platform guardrails (tenancy model, API contracts) early, while they're cheap, accepting you'll be partly wrong.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: What is Hume's problem of induction?
notes.back: No number of observed instances logically guarantees the next one, and justifying induction by its past success is circular. We rely on it by habit, not proof.
notes.extra: In practice: 'It has never failed in production' is induction; the next load pattern may differ.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: Popper's falsificationism: what makes a claim scientific?
notes.back: It is falsifiable: it forbids some possible observations. Confirmations are cheap; surviving severe tests is what counts.
notes.extra: In practice: State in advance what result would make you abandon a design hypothesis.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: What is the Duhem–Quine thesis, and why does it complicate falsification?
notes.back: Hypotheses are always tested together with auxiliary assumptions (instruments, background theory). A failed prediction refutes the bundle, and logic doesn't say which part to reject.
notes.extra: In practice: A failed load test may falsify the design, or the test harness, or the environment.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: Kuhn: what are normal science and a paradigm shift?
notes.back: Normal science solves puzzles inside an accepted paradigm. Anomalies pile up → crisis → a new paradigm wins, partly by persuasion and generational turnover. Rival paradigms disagree on what even counts as evidence.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: Lakatos: what distinguishes a progressive from a degenerating research programme?
notes.back: Progressive: its adjustments predict novel facts that are then confirmed. Degenerating: adjustments only patch known anomalies after the fact.
notes.extra: In practice: An architecture whose defenders only explain away each new incident is degenerating.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: Why does Lakatos judge research programmes over time rather than falsifying single hypotheses, as Popper proposed?
notes.back: Because of the Duhem–Quine problem: one failed prediction cannot say which assumption is wrong, so adjusting auxiliaries is legitimate. What matters is whether the adjustments predict novel facts (progressive) or only patch anomalies (degenerating).

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: What are immunising stratagems, and how do you test for them?
notes.back: Moves that shield a view from refutation: ad hoc auxiliaries, redefined terms, attacking the observer. Test: ask in advance what observation would count against it. No answer means it's unfalsifiable in practice.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: What is the underdetermination of theory by data?
notes.back: Several incompatible theories can fit the same evidence, so choosing between them needs extra criteria: simplicity, scope, fruitfulness.
notes.extra: In practice: Two root-cause theories can both fit the incident timeline; design a discriminating test.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: Inference to the best explanation (abduction): what is it, and the standard objection?
notes.back: Infer the hypothesis that would best explain the evidence (scope, mechanism, simplicity). Objection: 'best of a bad lot': the true explanation may not be among those considered.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: What is the theory-ladenness of observation?
notes.back: What counts as data depends on the concepts and instruments you bring. Observation reports carry assumptions, which can themselves be tested.
notes.extra: In practice: Dashboards show what someone decided to measure; the outage can live in what nobody instrumented.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: What is consilience, and why is it strong evidence?
notes.back: A theory gains strong support when it explains classes of facts it wasn't built to explain; independent lines of evidence converge.
notes.extra: Example: Newton's gravity covered tides, planets and falling bodies.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: What does Neurath's boat say about knowledge?
notes.back: We rebuild our beliefs like sailors rebuilding a ship at sea, plank by plank: there's no dry dock of certain foundations, but we can't doubt everything at once.
notes.extra: In practice: The same holds for live systems: you evolve them in production, never from a clean slate.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: What is reliabilism?
notes.back: A belief is justified if produced by a reliable process, whether or not the believer can articulate reasons. It underpins trusting instruments and track records.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: Feynman's 'cargo cult science': what norm does it lack?
notes.back: Reporting everything that could invalidate your result, not just what supports it: 'you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool.' Cargo cults copy the form without this norm.
notes.extra: In practice: A PoC report that lists only successes is cargo-cult evaluation.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: What is Peirce's fallibilism?
notes.back: Any belief may prove false, yet that alone is no reason for doubt. Beliefs are provisional but action-guiding; real doubt comes from a specific surprise. 'Do not block the way of inquiry.'

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: What is Chesterton's fence?
notes.back: Don't remove a fence until you know why it was put there. Existing practices often encode hidden evidence, usually about past failures.
notes.extra: In practice: That odd retry setting or firewall rule may be scar tissue from an old incident. Find out before deleting it.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: Chesterton's fence urges caution about removing practices, while the Semmelweis reflex is rejecting new evidence. How do you tell prudence from dogma?
notes.back: Ask whether anyone can state why the practice exists and what evidence would count against it. Unknown purpose: investigate before removing. Known purpose plus contrary evidence with a mechanism: change it.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: Aumann's agreement theorem: what does persistent disagreement between experts reveal?
notes.back: Rational agents with common priors who know each other's beliefs can't agree to disagree. So persistent disagreement means different priors, unshared information, or someone not updating.
notes.extra: In practice: In a deadlocked design debate, ask which of the three it is.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::03 Evidence & Belief Change
notes.front: Epistemic vs instrumental rationality: what's the difference?
notes.back: Epistemic: beliefs that track the truth. Instrumental: actions that achieve goals. Keeping them apart lets you notice when you believe something because it would be convenient.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::04 Probabilistic & Causal Reasoning
notes.front: Bayes in odds form: what makes something evidence, and how strong is it?
notes.back: Posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio, LR = P(E|H) / P(E|¬H). Evidence is anything more probable under one hypothesis than another; its strength is the LR.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::04 Probabilistic & Causal Reasoning
notes.front: Prior odds for a hypothesis are 1:100, and evidence has a likelihood ratio (LR) of 10. What are the posterior odds, and what does that say about strong-looking evidence?
notes.back: 1:10 (about 9%). Strong evidence against a low prior still leaves the hypothesis unlikely; the prior matters as much as the LR.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::04 Probabilistic & Causal Reasoning
notes.front: What is Cromwell's rule?
notes.back: Never assign probability exactly 0 or 1 to an empirical claim: then no evidence could ever move you.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::04 Probabilistic & Causal Reasoning
notes.front: Why does a prior of exactly 0 make learning impossible in odds form?
notes.back: Posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. If prior odds are 0, the product is 0 whatever the evidence, so no data can ever move you. That is why Cromwell's rule forbids it.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::04 Probabilistic & Causal Reasoning
notes.front: When is 'absence of evidence is not evidence of absence' false?
notes.back: Whenever you would expect to see evidence if the hypothesis were true. Not finding it is then evidence against, by the likelihood ratio.
notes.extra: In practice: No errors in logs that would certainly record the failure is real evidence; no errors in logs that don't capture it is not.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::04 Probabilistic & Causal Reasoning
notes.front: 'Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence': why, in Bayesian terms?
notes.back: A claim with low prior odds needs a large likelihood ratio to reach a credible posterior. Corollary: the more surprising the result, the more you should suspect error in the evidence.
notes.extra: In practice: A benchmark showing 10× speedup is more likely a measurement bug than a breakthrough.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::04 Probabilistic & Causal Reasoning
notes.front: What is the reference class problem?
notes.back: The probability you assign depends on which class you put the case in, and there's no unique right class: narrower is more relevant but has less data. Every base rate embeds a choice.
notes.extra: In practice: 'Migrations like ours' could mean same size, same stack or same org; show the estimate for more than one class.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::04 Probabilistic & Causal Reasoning
notes.front: Occam's razor: which justifications actually carry weight?
notes.back: Pragmatic: simpler theories are easier to test and use. Statistical: complex models fit noise and generalise worse (overfitting). 'Nature is simple' is unsupported.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::04 Probabilistic & Causal Reasoning
notes.front: Bradford Hill's viewpoints for causal inference: which one is necessary, and how should the rest be used?
notes.back: Only temporality (cause precedes effect) is necessary. The rest (strength, consistency, dose–response, plausibility…) are considerations to weigh, not a checklist.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::04 Probabilistic & Causal Reasoning
notes.front: What are the three rungs of Pearl's ladder of causation?
notes.back: 1 Association (seeing): P(y|x). 2 Intervention (doing): P(y|do(x)). 3 Counterfactuals (imagining). Observational data alone is rung 1; causal claims need a causal model or an experiment.
notes.extra: In practice: Correlating feature usage with retention is rung 1; an A/B test is rung 2.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::04 Probabilistic & Causal Reasoning
notes.front: Why is a randomised controlled trial privileged, and what are its two main limits?
notes.back: Randomisation makes treatment independent of all confounders, known and unknown. Limits: external validity (may not transfer) and it gives an average effect that can hide opposite individual effects.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::04 Probabilistic & Causal Reasoning
notes.front: Why did Ioannidis argue most published findings are false, and what are the fixes?
notes.back: Low prior odds, low power, flexible analysis and publication bias together produce mostly false positives. Fixes: preregistration, larger samples, shared data and code, replication.
notes.extra: In practice: Vendor benchmarks and internal 'success stories' have the same biases. Pre-define your PoC metrics.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::04 Probabilistic & Causal Reasoning
notes.front: What is Berkson's paradox (collider bias)?
notes.back: Selecting on a common effect of two independent causes creates a spurious correlation between them.
notes.extra: Example: Among escalated tickets, 'urgent' and 'complex' look negatively correlated, because either one gets a ticket escalated.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::04 Probabilistic & Causal Reasoning
notes.front: Two diseases are independent in the population, yet hospital patients show a negative correlation between them. Why?
notes.back: Hospital admission is a common effect of both: selecting on it creates a spurious link (collider bias). Among admitted patients, lacking one disease makes the other more likely.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::04 Probabilistic & Causal Reasoning
notes.front: Meehl: how do simple statistical formulas compare with expert clinical judgement?
notes.back: They match or beat experts in almost every domain studied. Experts are good at choosing the variables and bad at combining them consistently.
notes.extra: In practice: Score vendor evaluations with a fixed weighted rubric rather than a holistic gut call.

notes.deck: Adoption, Epistemics & Governance::04 Probabilistic & Causal Reasoning
notes.front: Value of information: when is evidence worth collecting?
notes.back: Only if it could change a decision. Evidence that would leave you doing the same thing is worthless for that decision, however interesting.
notes.extra: In practice: Before a two-month evaluation, ask which result would make you choose differently.

notes.front: Consequentialism vs deontology vs virtue ethics: where does each locate moral evaluation?
notes.back: Consequentialism: outcomes. Deontology: the act itself: duties, rights, constraints. Virtue ethics: the agent's character and practical wisdom (phronesis).
notes.extra: Most applied disputes are about which locus dominates when they conflict.

notes.front: Act vs rule utilitarianism: what's the difference, and what is the main defence of rules?
notes.back: Act: do whatever maximises utility in this case. Rule: follow rules whose general adoption maximises utility. Defence of rules: coordination, predictability and protection against case-by-case errors.
notes.extra: In practice: The same tension appears in policy-as-code: granting every 'beneficial' exception erodes the rule.

notes.front: Kant's categorical imperative: what are its two main formulations?
notes.back: Universal law: act only on maxims you could will everyone to follow. Humanity: treat persons always as ends, never merely as means (the root of consent and dignity requirements).

notes.front: What is Rawls's veil of ignorance, and what does it yield?
notes.back: Choose rules without knowing your own position. Rawls: equal basic liberties, and inequalities only if they benefit the least advantaged (difference principle).
notes.analogy: Cutting a cake when someone else picks the first slice.
notes.extra: In practice: Design platform policies (quotas, priorities) as if you didn't know which team you'd be on.

notes.front: What is Hume's is–ought gap, and what does it imply for data-driven decisions?
notes.back: You can't validly derive a normative conclusion from purely descriptive premises. Data can't settle values; a value premise must be stated explicitly.
notes.extra: In practice: 'Users click it more' doesn't by itself establish that you should ship it.

notes.front: What is Mill's harm principle?
notes.back: Power may be exercised over someone against their will only to prevent harm to others, not for their own good. The hard part is defining 'harm'.

notes.front: Berlin: negative vs positive liberty?
notes.back: Negative: freedom from interference. Positive: self-mastery, the capacity to act. Berlin warned positive liberty can justify coercion 'for your own good'.
notes.extra: In practice: Does a guardrail that removes options protect teams or restrict them?

notes.front: What is Pettit's republican liberty as non-domination?
notes.back: Freedom means no one holds arbitrary power over you, even if they never use it. Power must be constrained, contestable and accountable.
notes.analogy: A kind master's slave is still unfree.
notes.extra: In practice: A platform team that could change tenant quotas at will dominates tenants even if it never does; publish rules and an appeal path.

notes.front: What is the doctrine of double effect (trolley problem), and why does it matter for automated systems?
notes.back: Harm that is a foreseen side-effect of a good act may be permissible; harm used as a means is not. An automated system's objective must encode or ignore this distinction.
notes.extra: Most people would pull the switch (kill 1 to save 5) but not push someone off the footbridge.

notes.front: Hardin's tragedy of the commons vs Ostrom's findings: what did Ostrom show?
notes.back: Hardin: shared resources are inevitably overused unless privatised or state-controlled. Ostrom: communities sustainably self-govern commons with the right rules. Hardin described open access; real commons have rules.
notes.extra: In practice: A shared cluster without quotas or showback gets over-provisioned by every team rationally. Fix it with rules (quotas, chargeback), not appeals to consideration.

notes.text: Ostrom's design principles for durable commons include: {{c1::clear boundaries}} (who may use it), those affected {{c2::can modify the rules}}, {{c3::monitoring by accountable monitors}}, {{c4::graduated sanctions}}, and cheap conflict resolution.
notes.extra: In practice: Shared CI capacity or clusters: defined tenants, team-level say in quota rules, visible usage, warnings before hard limits.

notes.front: What is subsidiarity?
notes.back: Decide at the lowest level competent to decide; higher levels step in only where lower ones can't achieve the goal.
notes.extra: In practice: Teams own service-level choices; the platform sets only the guardrails teams can't set for themselves.

notes.front: What are Weber's three types of legitimate authority?
notes.back: Traditional (always been so), charismatic (the leader's qualities), legal-rational (rules enacted by proper procedure, applied impersonally).
notes.extra: Automated decision systems inherit legal-rational authority's demand for procedural regularity.

notes.text: Fuller's inner morality of law: rules must be general, public, prospective, clear, non-contradictory, stable, {{c1::possible to comply with}}, and {{c2::congruent with how they are actually enforced}}.
notes.extra: In practice: A useful checklist for any rule-enforcing system, including admission policies. A rule nobody can comply with is a trap, not an obligation ('ought implies can').

notes.front: What is the governance lesson of separation of powers for technical systems?
notes.back: Liberty requires that making, executing and judging rules be in different hands so each checks the others. By analogy: one actor shouldn't build, deploy and audit the same system.

notes.front: What does Arrow's impossibility theorem say?
notes.back: No ranked voting rule over three or more options can satisfy all of: unrestricted domain, Pareto efficiency, independence of irrelevant alternatives, non-dictatorship. Every preference aggregation is a trade-off.
notes.extra: In practice: No weighted scoring of stakeholder priorities is neutral; make the weighting an explicit decision.

notes.front: Condorcet's jury theorem: when does majority voting get more accurate with group size, and when does it fail?
notes.back: When each voter is independently more likely than not to be right. It fails if competence is below ½ or if votes are correlated (shared information, herding).
notes.extra: In practice: Independent estimates first, discussion second, or the group just amplifies the loudest view.

notes.front: 100 voters each have a 70% chance of being right but all rely on the same news source. Does the jury theorem's accuracy gain hold?
notes.back: No. The theorem needs independent votes. Shared information makes errors correlated, so the group is only about as reliable as the source, however large it is.

notes.front: When is regulation of an externality justified rather than private bargaining?
notes.back: When costs fall on third parties and bargaining is infeasible (many victims, diffuse harm, high transaction costs). With low transaction costs, bargaining can fix it (Coase).

notes.front: What is precommitment, and why can removing your own options be rational?
notes.back: Binding your future self against predictable temptation increases welfare: Ulysses tied to the mast, constitutions, supermajority rules.
notes.analogy: Ulysses tied himself to the mast so he could hear the Sirens without steering onto the rocks.
notes.extra: In practice: Error budgets and change freezes agreed in advance precommit teams before the deadline pressure arrives.

notes.front: What is Popper's piecemeal social engineering?
notes.back: Reform through small, reversible changes whose effects can be tested, rather than utopian blueprints. Governance as a falsifiable experiment.
notes.extra: In practice: Roll out new policy as a dry-run or to one tenant first, measure, then widen.

notes.front: Precautionary vs proactionary principle: how do they differ?
notes.back: Precautionary: serious or irreversible risk justifies preventive action despite uncertainty (burden on the proponent). Proactionary: forgone innovation is a cost too (burden on the restrictor). They allocate the burden of proof differently.

notes.front: Lessig: what are the four modalities of regulation, and why does 'code is law' matter?
notes.back: Law, norms, the market and architecture (code). Architecture regulates without enforcement or consent and is often invisible as regulation, so design choices are political choices.
notes.extra: In practice: A platform default (e.g. no public load balancers) regulates teams more effectively than any written policy.

notes.front: What is Nissenbaum's contextual integrity?
notes.back: Privacy is the appropriate flow of information according to the norms of the context where it was shared. A violation is a flow that breaches those norms, even if each party 'consented'.
notes.extra: Example: Health data flowing from a wellness app to an employer.

notes.front: Why can't a classifier satisfy all common fairness criteria at once?
notes.back: When base rates differ between groups, it can't simultaneously be calibrated and have equal false-positive and false-negative rates. Choosing the fairness metric is an ethical decision, not a technical one.

notes.front: Two groups have different base rates and a model is perfectly calibrated for both. What happens to its error rates, and who decides what to do?
notes.back: Its false-positive and false-negative rates must differ between groups (unless prediction is perfect). Which criterion to give up is a value judgement for stakeholders, not a technical fix.

notes.front: What are the problem of many hands and the responsibility gap?
notes.back: Many hands: in large organisations so many people contribute that no one is responsible. Responsibility gap: with learning systems no one can foresee behaviour well enough to be fairly blamed. Both argue for designing accountability in advance.
notes.extra: In practice: Name an owner for every automated decision path before launch, not in the post-mortem.

notes.front: What is value-sensitive design?
notes.back: Treating values as design requirements through three iterative investigations: conceptual (which stakeholders and values), empirical (how they experience it), technical (which choices support the values).

notes.front: What does meaningful human control require, and what undermines it?
notes.back: Humans who can understand, intervene in and answer for a system's actions, not merely be present. Undermined by automation bias: people defer to automated outputs even when wrong.
notes.extra: In practice: An approver who rubber-stamps 200 AI-generated changes a day gives legitimacy without control.
notes.source: Santoni de Sio & van den Hoven

notes.front: Procedural vs substantive justice: why does the right to reasons matter for automated decisions?
notes.back: Procedural: fair process (notice, hearing, reasons, appeal). Substantive: correct outcome. Reasons enable contestation and check arbitrariness; GDPR Art. 22 extends this to solely automated decisions with significant effects.
